articles.title: Netanyahu falls short of majority as Israel faces three possible paths to a new government
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition falls short of a majority as Arab parties surge to 19 seats, giving the opposition a potential 67-seat block.
articles.body: TEL AVIV, Israel - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition remained well short of a parliamentary majority Thursday as newly counted ballots showed a dramatic surge in support for Arab parties, potentially giving the opposition enough votes to challenge his control of parliament. With 93.8% of ballots counted as of 4 a.m. ET Thursday (10 a.m. local time in Israel), including votes from the double-envelope count, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc was projected to win 53 seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset, compared with 48 for the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. The two predominantly Arab parties were projected to secure a combined 19 seats, bringing the potential anti-Netanyahu parliamentary majority to 67. The updated figures showed Netanyahu's Likud remaining the largest individual party with 26 seats, followed by Eisenkot's Yashar party with 21 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett's Beyachad party with 12. The figures remain preliminary. NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE The results leave neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with the 61 seats required to form a government independently, raising the prospect of difficult coalition negotiations or another election. The biggest shift came from Israel's Arab voters, whose turnout surged compared with previous elections, potentially reshaping the country's political balance. Arab voter participation reached approximately 80%, compared with 53.2% in the 2022 election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute. The 2026 figure remains preliminary. The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra'am was projected to secure eight. Together, their 19 seats would nearly double the Arab parties' representation from the 10 seats they won in 2022. Overall voter turnout reached 77.7% by the official 10 p.m. closing time on election night, the highest level at that hour since 1999, according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. The increased Arab participation could prove decisive in determining the next government's composition. Although Eisenkot and several other opposition leaders ruled out including Arab parties in their governing coalition during the campaign, their parliamentary support could allow the opposition to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, and gain greater control over the legislative agenda even before a new government is formed. IRAN IS TRYING TO ‘CREATE A ROT FROM WITHIN’ THROUGH ‘INFORMATION WARFARE,’ ANALYST WARNS Qatar allegations intensify political battle The political stakes intensified Thursday following a Channel 12 report alleging that substantial sums originating in Qatar may have been transferred to influence voter participation in Arab communities. According to N12, some of the funds allegedly traveled through financial channels previously used to transfer money to terrorist organizations, including currency exchanges. The allegations have not been independently substantiated, and investigators have yet to establish whether foreign financing occurred or whether election-related crimes were committed. Channel 12 reported that Shin Bet Director David Zini presented intelligence concerning suspected foreign interference to Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, prompting the judge to order an investigation. In a letter published by N12, Sohlberg instructed the domestic security agency to investigate the allegations and identify evidence that could either substantiate or disprove them. He requested findings within one week, citing the limited time available during the election count. The judge's letter did not publicly identify Qatar as the suspected foreign actor. That identification came from N12's reporting. Qatar strongly denied the allegations Thursday, accusing Israeli politicians of attempting to drag the Gulf nation into Israel's domestic political disputes following the election. "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr. Majed Al-Ansari wrote on X. Al-Ansari accused Israeli politicians and their allies in the media of launching a "disinformation campaign," saying Qatar had been accused of financing Netanyahu, the Israeli left and now Arab voters. "If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel," he wrote. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians," Al-Ansari added, insisting that Qatar had no involvement in Israel's electoral process and would continue its diplomatic and humanitarian efforts in the region. Acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne also rejected the allegations in a letter to Yesh Atid MK Vladimir Beliak, who sits on the committee. "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity." Israel's Shin Bet security agency clarified Thursday that the intelligence behind the investigation was gathered independently and did not originate from any political party. It said no one outside the agency, except Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, had access to the information before the election ended. The agency stressed that the investigation remains ongoing and warned against drawing premature conclusions. The investigation "does not cast aspersions on or accuse an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and lawfully," the Shin Bet said in a statement translated from Hebrew. The agency also confirmed that Shin Bet Director David Zini had briefed Netanyahu, Eisenkot and opposition leader Yair Lapid on the allegations, with Sohlberg's approval. ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW But the allegations have already become part of the political confrontation over whether opposition parties should cooperate with Arab lawmakers. Netanyahu and Likud had challenged the legitimacy of the Arab parties' electoral gains. On Wednesday, before the latest Qatari allegations emerged, Likud accused Arab parties of stealing the election through alleged voter fraud, accusations that had not been substantiated. In a statement Thursday, Likud argued that the suspected foreign interference made cooperation with the Arab parties unacceptable. "After it became clear that foreign actors attempted to take control of the Knesset, it is obvious that no Zionist party must cooperate with Ra'am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker using votes bought with cash, or establish a government dangerous to Israel," the party said. The assertion that parliamentary seats were obtained through purchased votes has not been established by the investigation. Hauser Tov, a political reporter for Israel's Haaretz newspaper, argued on X that the statement revealed Likud's immediate political objective: preventing the opposition from using its potential parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker. Israeli journalist Amir Tibon wrote on X, "The main reason they want to prevent this is so that the Knesset won't vote to establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7." He argued that such an investigation could examine Qatari involvement in Gaza and Israel. Eisenkot responded to the allegations Thursday, after meeting with Israel Security Agency (Shin Bet) Director David Zini. "Foreign involvement in Israel is unacceptable and profoundly serious, particularly when it involves a country that funds and supports Hamas," Eisenkot said. "It is serious when it occurs in the Prime Minister’s Office, and it is serious if it occurs in the electoral process." He called on the Shin Bet to investigate the allegations thoroughly and take the strongest possible action against anyone found to have attempted to compromise the election's integrity. Eisenkot also accused Netanyahu and his allies of conducting "an illegitimate influence operation targeting the Israeli public," claiming its purpose was to delay the publication of the results and undermine the legitimacy of the newly elected Knesset. Israeli political commentator Amit Segal also cautioned against assuming the allegations would lead to the cancellation of election results. "The likelihood of the entire election being invalidated is extremely slim, given the time constraints," Segal wrote on X. He suggested the developments could instead intensify discussions about a unity government or another election. Meanwhile, Democrats party leader Yair Golan urged opposition leaders to move quickly toward forming a new government. "The people have spoken. Sixty-seven seats demanded change," Golan wrote Thursday on X, adding that he intended to spend the day meeting with political partners and coalition negotiators. "I intend to leave no stone unturned, act in every possible way and do everything necessary to fulfill the voters' will," he added. The comments underscored the central question emerging from the election: whether parties united in their opposition to Netanyahu can overcome their differences, particularly over cooperation with Arab lawmakers. Could Trump help broker a unity government? Another possibility is a national unity coalition involving Netanyahu's Likud and Eisenkot's Yashar party, potentially excluding the Arab parties and Netanyahu's far-right allies. Such an arrangement could also align with the preferences of figures close to President Donald Trump, who publicly endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election. According to Ynet diplomatic correspondent Itamar Eichner, sources close to Trump said the president wants to ensure that far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is excluded from the next Israeli government, with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich potentially excluded as well. A separate Ynet report said Trump associates had contacted Israeli political figures to assess the prospects for a unity government and expressed a preference for a stable coalition without Ben-Gvir. Trump himself has not publicly endorsed a specific unity arrangement. Asked Wednesday by Axios whether he would become involved in efforts to establish a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said, "I will take a look." A unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot would face substantial obstacles. Eisenkot repeatedly pledged during the campaign not to join a Netanyahu-led government, while Netanyahu's far-right partners have warned against efforts to exclude them. The ultra-Orthodox parties present another potential route to a parliamentary majority. Netanyahu's projected 53 seats include 14 held by Shas and United Torah Judaism, which have traditionally aligned with him. Those 14 seats, combined with Eisenkot's projected 48-seat opposition bloc, would mathematically produce a 62-seat majority. But such an arrangement would face major disagreements over military conscription, as Eisenkot has pledged to expand mandatory service to ultra-Orthodox men, while the religious parties have sought to preserve exemptions for yeshiva students. Political divisions within Eisenkot's own bloc would present additional obstacles to such a coalition. For now, the foreign interference allegations remain under investigation, while the election results continue to show Netanyahu's existing coalition without the parliamentary majority required to govern on its own. articles.title: CCTV shows frying pan used to stop Huntingdon train attacker
articles.summary: A train crew member shows "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives", a court hears.
articles.body:
CCTV footage of a crew member using a frying pan to fend off a knifeman aboard a train has been shown in court.

Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Samir Zitouni showed "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives and defend others", during the mass stabbing on the Doncaster to London King's Cross train.

Jurors at Cambridge Crown Court saw footage of Zitouni using the pan against Anthony Williams, before the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.

Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies attempting to murder 10 people aboard the train, three people in Peterborough the day before and a boy at a London railway station.

The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.

On the second day of the trial, Paxton told jurors the attack on Zitouni was "prolonged, persistent and brutal".

Zitouni was said to have told the defendant: "We love you, we can help you."

Other CCTV footage played in court showed people fleeing the train.

Zitouni, in what Paxton called a "blood-soaked shirt", appeared "to be one of the last off the train", and Paxton said he fell "between, essentially, the gap between the train and the platform".

The court heard both of Zitouni's lungs had been punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.

Paxton earlier said one of the passengers, Raza Aslam, had grabbed a frying pan, but was stabbed in the hand by Williams.

He said Zitouni started throwing things at the defendant and "saved" Aslam's life.

Jurors also heard that Aslam told police Williams "had the greatest delight on his face".

Aslam said: "I saw his eyes expand with pleasure. I saw the contempt on his face, like a person who's high.

"He was just loving every single moment. He loved seeing us in desperation."

Paxton also told the jury how there was hand-to-hand fighting on the train.

He said Sachin Balakrishnan was stabbed in the forearm and chest, puncturing a lung and "being just centimetres from his heart".

Commenting on the CCTV footage, Paxton said: "You can see the panic, you can see the fear in the faces of those fleeing.

"In this storm of violence, and even when gripped by fear, many there on that train helped others and, as we will see, some stood tall, quite literally, against the defendant's violent onslaught."

Jurors also heard how Scott Green had been travelling on the train with his dog, Poppy.

Paxton said: "He thought he was going to lose his life on the train when the defendant tried to stab him for the third time.

"It seems, members of the jury, that Poppy the dog, for Mr Green at least, saved the day and sent the defendant running off.

"You will hear that in an unrelated incident the defendant had previously been bitten by a dog."

During Thursday's evidence, the court was also told of an attack on 73-year-old David Presland, who had been stabbed in the back while on his hands and knees.

Presland said he had been "helped by someone he knew as Kevin" - believed to be Kevin Deely, another of those Williams is accused of attempting to murder.

Paxton told the court the events were "all over in about five minutes", adding: "In that time, 10 men are stabbed by one man, this defendant, Mr Williams."

Williams is accused of attempting to murder Aslam, Balakrishnan, Deely, Green, Presland and Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on the Saturday evening, along with Scott Bletcher, Stephen Crean, Jonathan Gjoshe and Michael Paffett.

He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.

articles.title: China’s Communist Party expels 33 officials in post-Mao era record purge
articles.summary: China’s Communist Party confirmed a wave of expulsions of senior officials ​and unexpectedly elevated top general Zhang Shengmin ‌to the elite Politburo.
articles.body: China’s Communist Party confirmed a wave of expulsions of senior officials ​and unexpectedly elevated top general Zhang Shengmin ‌to the elite Politburo this week, during a four-day conclave focused on tightening internal discipline. The gathering, the party’s “Fifth ​Plenum” since the current leadership cohort was formed ​in 2022, also set the 21st Party ⁠Congress for the second half of 2027 in ​Beijing, effectively opening China’s tightly choreographed, twice-a-decade contest ​for top leadership posts. The meeting of the party’s Central Committee, the largest of its top decision-making bodies, saw the highest ​rate of absences in the post-Mao era, ​underscoring the scale of President Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption campaign and ‌wider ⁠political shake-up. In total, 279 full and alternate members of the leadership body attended the gathering this week, compared with the 376 originally named in 2022, ​a summary ​of the ⁠proceedings dispatched by the official Xinhua news agency showed. This means over a ​quarter of the original cohort was ​absent, many ⁠of them due to purges. The plenum formally confirmed the expulsion of 33 officials from the party, ⁠including ​former Politburo members Ma Xingrui and ​Zhang Youxia, former senior diplomat Liu Jianchao and former industry ​minister Jin Zhuanglong.

articles.title: Jacksepticeye: YouTuber talks Hitman, Bloodborne and new projects
articles.summary: He got famous playing video games but now you're more likely to see Seán McLoughlin in one.
articles.body:
The world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.

He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.

Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.

BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.

McLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.

After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.

He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.

Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.

As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him.

He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans.

"If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin.

"If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."

It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.

He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it.

"This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.

Earlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.

Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials.

McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it.

He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly.

"If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says.

"They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."

McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about.

"I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says.

"So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."

Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.

Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.

McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely".

"Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.

The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.

Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.

Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.

So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?

"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says.

"But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."

Physical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.

He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released".

"I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says.

"It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything.

"But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."

McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries.

"Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says.

"So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days.

"It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."

McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.

The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.

"I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.

And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes.

"I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says.

"Because I think there's too much of that in the world."

articles.title: Spain Urda train crash: Shock of tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
articles.summary: The latest train crash will pile pressure on the government of Pedro Sánchez, one month before the general election.
articles.body:
The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.

But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls.

"You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60.

He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital.

"There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."

Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."

Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine.

"One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.

Similar scenes of grief played out only nine months ago in the southern village of Adamuz, when a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people.

Now, in the town of Urda, just like Adamuz, awful stories are combined with acts of kindness and solidarity.

Locals turned out to help the injured, bringing blankets, food and water to a nearby sports hall that was converted into a makeshift hospital for much of the day.

"We all started to turn out to help and we organised ourselves as best we could," said Rosa María Domínguez, a local woman, who described the scene as "a horror film".

However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.

Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.

The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.

This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.

On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.

Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.

Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.

Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.

Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".

One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.

Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.

After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."

And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.

articles.title: Trump seeks prosecution of Democrat Mary Peltola over alleged scheme to field Dan Sullivan namesake in Alaska
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has called for the removal and prosecution of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola after a report alleged that people linked
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has called for the removal and prosecution of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola after a report alleged that people linked to her campaign discussed recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican Senator Dan Sullivan to potentially confuse voters in Alaska.Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy has also announced plans to launch a criminal investigation into whether the alleged scheme violated state election laws.The controversy follows a New York Times report published on Wednesday that cited interviews, text messages and documents indicating that Peltola's campaign aides and officials linked to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) discussed recruiting candidates named Dan Sullivan to run against the Republican incumbent.Trump called for Peltola and Daniel J Sullivan Jr, a retired schoolteacher who is challenging Senator Sullivan, to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. In a social media post, he accused Democrats of election fraud and described the alleged operation as voter fraud.Dunleavy said he was directing Alaska's Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged plan warranted criminal charges or civil action.“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” the governor said, adding that anyone found to have broken the law must be held accountable.The allegations have surfaced days before the November 3 midterm elections, with the Alaska Senate race among the contests that could determine control of the US Senate.What the report allegedAccording to the New York Times, the effort began in 2025, when a Peltola aide was asked to identify Alaskans named Dan Sullivan. The newspaper reported that campaign aides and senior Democratic operatives discussed recruiting candidates who could potentially split support for the Republican senator.The effort eventually focused on Daniel J Sullivan Jr, a retired schoolteacher from Petersburg, Alaska, who has no previous political experience. He qualified for the November general election after the Alaska Supreme Court overturned a state elections official's decision to disqualify him from the primary ballot.The official had concluded that his candidacy had been filed with the purpose of confusing or misleading voters. However, the state Supreme Court ruled that he was qualified to run.The Times report cited interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, and other people familiar with the alleged plan. Rios told the newspaper that Peltola knew about the operation but did not participate directly. The newspaper also reported that Rios later sought to retract her statements.Peltola's campaign has denied involvement in recruiting either Sullivan candidate. The DSCC has also denied recruiting Daniel J Sullivan Jr, despite the report's account of discussions between committee staff and Peltola's campaign.Daniel J Sullivan Jr has maintained that he entered the race independently and had no contact with Peltola's campaign.Political and legal falloutRepublican Senator Dan Sullivan's campaign accused Peltola, her advisers and Democratic operatives of colluding to mislead voters. Alaska Senator Lisa Murkowski, who has endorsed Sullivan and is a longtime friend of Peltola, also called for an explanation from the Democratic candidate.The controversy comes as the Trump administration pursues a separate legal challenge seeking to block certification of a possible Peltola victory, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.However, legal experts said the allegations reported by the Times would not necessarily affect the outcome of that lawsuit. They noted that while recruiting candidates to split an opponent's vote can be viewed as a dirty political tactic, it is generally legal.The two Sullivans are among four candidates contesting the Alaska Senate seat under the state's ranked-choice voting system, in which voters rank candidates by preference and votes can be transferred when a candidate is eliminated.Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman, is challenging Sullivan as Democrats seek to win control of the Senate in the November midterm elections.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel’s anti-Qatar campaign bleeds into elections
articles.summary: Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman rejects ‘disinformation’ amid allegations by some Israelis of voting interference.
articles.body:
As Israel awaits the final results of its highly contested elections , some political figures have sought to drag Qatar into the fray with claims of voting interference – an accusation Doha rejects.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and media outlets associated with it have, without evidence, accused Qatar of sending money to Arab parties in Israel for get-out-the-vote drives.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman on Thursday categorically denied the allegations of interference or funding of any activities aimed at influencing the election results.

“We reject the accusations made by certain Israeli politicians and their contacts in the media, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes following this week’s elections,” Majed al-Ansari said in a post on X.

The unsubstantiated Israeli claims, which the spokesperson described as “ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure”, are the latest in a long-running campaign against Qatar.

Netanyahu has previously boasted about attacking Qatar in September 2025 during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza while Israeli influence experts and political advisers also worked on a secret campaign targeting Qatar in the weeks after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israel.

“[Some Israeli politicians] accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote. If these claims were to be believed, Qatar would apparently own all of Israel,” al-Ansari said.

Partial results indicated that Netanyahu’s bloc would not secure a majority in the Knesset in Tuesday’s parliamentary elections. Those results showed the two Arab lists securing a record number of seats in the new parliament, but the main parties have rejected the idea of partnering with them.

Despite the latest claims, Dean Livine, the acting director for Israel’s Central Elections Committee, has rejected allegations of foreign interference in the elections. “The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded,” he wrote in a letter to an MP and fellow committee member.

“The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures,” al-Ansari said, adding that Qatar should “not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians”.

The Foreign Ministry spokesman said some Israeli politicians, instead of shifting attention onto Qatar, “would be better off focusing on their own voters, improving people’s everyday lives, and undoing the damage they’ve created in the region”.

He reiterated that Qatar has “no involvement” in Israel’s political or electoral competition.

“These are internal Israeli matters in which we do not interfere, and we will not accept any attempt to draw Qatar into its domestic political disputes.”

Qatar is a key mediator in the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians and played a central role in talks to halt Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Doha is also leading mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran to end the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Al-Ansari said the latest accusations would not distract Doha from its “important role as a mediator, our diplomatic and humanitarian efforts, our support for the Palestinian people, or our commitment to a just and comprehensive peace and regional stability.”

articles.title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
articles.summary: Opponents have questioned the Budget's lack of detail on welfare reform, with the prime minister not outlining a timetable for any reductions.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.

Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.

Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."

He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".

The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.

When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."

But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".

The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.

Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.

These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.

The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.

Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.

He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."

Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.

"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."

Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.

Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".

She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."

Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.

Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.

Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.

The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030 , and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

articles.title: Barbara Barrie, Oscar-nominated actor, dies with medical assistance at 95
articles.summary: Oscar-nominated actor Barbara Barrie died Wednesday at her New York City home with medical assistance.
articles.body: Oscar-nominated actor Barbara Barrie died Wednesday at her New York City home with medical assistance. She was 95. Her agent, Gary Gersh, confirmed to NBC News in a statement Thursday that Barrie’s death was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying law, of which she was a proponent and advocate.” The law took effect on Aug. 5 and allows terminally ill adults with less than six months to live to obtain a self-administered prescription medication to end their lives. Barrie’s daughter, Jane Harnick, said her mother had been diagnosed with terminal cancer but had always advocated “for the right to die on your own terms.” “Her whole life, even before she was ill with anything, she always said, ‘When the time comes, I want to just take something and go to sleep.’ She used to talk about that,” Harnick said in a phone interview. She said the law going into effect in August was perfect timing because her mother “did not want to get to the point of having us watch her suffer,” she said. “She is just a huge proponent of the law and was so grateful to be able to do it her way,” Harnick said, adding that the family supported her “100%.” Harnick said one of the most important things to her mother was people being able to discuss medically assisted deaths “without judgment.” “She was 95. She had done everything she wanted in life. She had her family. She had her house. She lived in her favorite city, and she experienced it all to the fullest. And she was ready. She was so ready,” she said. According to The New York Times, Barrie had also been living with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of interstitial lung disease that causes breathing issues, fatigue and weight loss. “I have a very full, active life, but what lies ahead is unknown and yet known at the same time,” Barrie told Playbill in a 2014 interview about her lung disease diagnosis. “I am living full steam ahead and am now trying to help other people do the same.” Barrie was best known for her role as Evelyn Stohler in the 1979 movie “Breaking Away,” which earned her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination. In 1971, Barrie was nominated for a Tony Award for best featured actress in a musical for “Company,” Broadway.com reported. Her other stage credits included “The Selling of the President” and “The Prisoner of Second Avenue.” She also received Emmy nominations for her roles in “Law & Order” and “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” and “Breaking Away,” a television series based on the movie. articles.title: European Central Bank President Lagarde to step down early
articles.summary: Christine Lagarde will leave the post in February, nine months before the end of her eight-year term.
articles.body:
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde will step down months before her term ends, kicking off a race to succeed her against a turbulent backdrop in the eurozone.

Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will leave the post on February 7, about nine months before the scheduled end of her eight-year term. She said in a filmed statement posted on X that she was leaving “with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future”.

The move gives European Union leaders time to choose her successor before April’s French presidential election, which polls have suggested far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win.

The timing could allow current European Council members, including French President Emmanuel Macron, to take part in appointing Lagarde’s successor before France’s vote.

Macron, who is not allowed to run again, thanked Lagarde in a post on X for “the determined action she led at the head of the European Central Bank” during “a period marked by numerous crises”.

“The transition at the head of the ECB must now be prepared in an orderly and balanced manner with our European partners,” the leader of the eurozone’s second-largest economy added.

However, Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament, warned: “If the impression arises that such a departure is timed around national elections, it damages trust in an institution that must stand above any domestic political calculation.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leader of the eurozone’s largest economy, said Lagarde had led the bank “with great aplomb during challenging times”, and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen thanked Lagarde “for everything you have done for Europe and the euro”.

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure praised her tenure. “Christine Lagarde has been an exceptional President of the ECB. As Europe navigated through crises and difficult times, she brilliantly modernised and strengthened the institution,” he posted on social media.

Marcel Fratzscher, president of the German Institute for Economic Research, told the Reuters news agency the early exit gives governments “an opportunity to appoint a successor who will safeguard European values and protect the ECB’s independence”.

Markets appeared unfazed. “Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde and be quite similar, whoever takes over,” Simon Dangoor, head of fixed income macro investing at Goldman Sachs told Reuters.

Lagarde, appointed in October 2019, steered the bank through the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the United States-Israel war on Iran.

The ECB faced criticism for responding too slowly to the 2022 inflation surge, caused by post-pandemic supply chain bottlenecks and the war on Ukraine. Inflation is currently running at almost double the bank’s 2 percent target amid worries over France’s public finances.

A former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, Lagarde arrived in Frankfurt in 2019 as the first ECB chief with no formal economics training or central banking experience, prompting some market participants to warn of a “credibility risk”.

In March 2020 as the pandemic shook sovereign debt markets, she said the bank was not there to narrow the gap between Italian and German borrowing costs. She went on to show that political diplomacy could steer a central bank through historic shocks.

Sources told the AFP news agency that leaving early would give Lagarde “greater freedom to express her views”. She has hinted she could campaign in the French presidential race, saying a European voice was needed in the debate.

articles.title: Lost a toenail while running? Here’s how to treat and prevent runner’s toe, according to doctors
articles.summary: Runner’s toe ranges in severity from discolored nails to toenails falling off. Doctors explain the best treatments for runner’s toe and how to prevent it while training.
articles.body: I’ll admit it: I’ve had three cases of runner’s toe this year, and I lost my toenail each time. It’s a common issue among runners, especially those logging long distances while marathon training or doing the race itself. The good news? It’s totally treatable and completely preventable, according to doctors I talked to. Read on to learn how to treat runner’s toe and prevent it from happening again, whether you have a black and blue nail or one that fell off. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What is runner’s toe? Runner’s toe is a commonly used term for a subungual hematoma, a.k.a. bleeding under the nail bed, says Dr. Jacob Wynes, a podiatric surgeon and an associate professor of foot and ankle surgery for the University of Maryland School of Medicine. You’ll see red, purple and black-ish discoloration under your toenail, which can sometimes be painful or cause throbbing pressure. Runner’s toe may eventually lead to the affected toenails partially or fully falling off. The condition can impact any toe on your foot, but you most commonly get it on your longest toe, which is either the big toe or second toe for most people. While a subungual hematoma is colloquially called “runner’s toe,” runners aren’t the only people who get it: Anyone can, especially if they’re wearing poorly fitting shoes, says Wynes. In terms of physical activity, runners, soccer players, football players, tennis players, skiers, hikers and golfers are most prone to “runner’s toe.” You can also get a subungual hematoma if you drop something on your toe or stub it, says Dr. Kristin Hullings, an assistant professor of clinical orthopaedic surgery and sports medicine at Temple University’s Lewis Katz School of Medicine — in those cases, since the bleeding is caused by sudden rather than gradual trauma, see a doctor to make sure you didn’t also fracture or break your toe. What causes runner’s toe? Runner’s toe is caused by repetitive trauma to the toenails during running, says Dr. Rull James Toussaint, the chief of the foot and ankle division in the department of orthopaedic surgery and sports medicine at the University of Florida College of Medicine. Running downhill, high mileage, wearing loose shoes that cause your feet to slide around, wearing tight shoes that squeeze your feet, long toenails, heat buildup and sweat/moisture buildup all increase friction and pressure between your toes and the top or front of a shoe. Eventually, this increased, forceful toe to shoe contact can rupture blood vessels in your nail bed, leading blood to collect under the nail plate, says Hullings. How do you treat runner’s toe? Runner’s toe ranges in severity, so treatment plans do, too. Below, I break down how to treat minor to moderate cases and the supplies you’ll need, according to doctors. Regardless of how severe your runner’s toe is, it’s crucial that you identify what caused it and correct it to prevent the condition from worsening or reoccurring — follow these prevention tips. Finally, if you have significant and/or worsening pain or swelling, see your doctor — there’s more information on that in the FAQ section here. If your toenail is still intact If you have blood buildup under your toenail, but it’s still intact, not loose, you aren’t experiencing pain and there’s no exposed nail bed, your runner’s toe will likely go away on its own as the nail grows out, says Toussaint. Focus on preventing runner’s toe from getting worse or happening again — I included prevention tips here. The toenail might eventually get loose and start shedding (falling off). In that case, see doctors’ treatment advice below. If your toenail partially or fully falls off If your toenail partially or fully falls off, your goal is to keep the exposed nail bed clean and protected to prevent infection and promote regrowth, says Hullings. Exactly how you do so is a bit different in each circumstance: Because a fully detached nail leaves the nail bed completely exposed, it’s fragile and needs extra care, while a partially detached nail is more protected, so the process is simpler. That said, the core principals are the same — here’s what to do. Clean the affected toe Whether you have a partially or fully detached nail, first cleanse the affected toe to remove any dirt, says Wynes. You can use mild soap and water or a saline solution. NeilMed’s saline solution is made with 0.9 percent sodium chloride and water, making it a gentle yet effective wash. It comes in a bottle with a nozzle that sprays in any direction, even when it’s upside down, which is helpful when reaching your toes. Trim away loose parts of the nail If you have a partially detached toenail, leave the attached portion in place — it acts as a protective splint for the nail that’s left over, and promotes healing with a lower risk for infection, says Hullings. You should trim away loose, snagging edges, however, to prevent them from catching on socks, pant legs and sheets — you don’t want to end up with another open wound to worry about. Trim as little as possible to preserve as much of the leftover nail as you can, but just enough to make sure there’s smooth edges, says Wynes. I find using a cuticle cutter to snip my partially detached toenail’s loose, sharp edges to be more efficient than using standard nail cutters. The head of the cuticle cutters are smaller and narrower, allowing me to make tiny, precise clips and avoid getting rid of too much nail. I’ve owned Tweezerman’s stainless steel Rockhard Cuticle Nippers for years and they’ve always stayed sharp. You only need to put light pressure on the handle to make a trim, and they’re designed for right- and left-handed people to use. Apply a topical ointment Applying a topical antibiotic ointment to the exposed nail bed prevents infection, keeps the area moist and promotes healing, says Wynes. Neosporin’s ointment uses three antibiotics to kill germs and prevent infection for up to 24 hours post-application, according to the brand. Its formula also helps skin stay hydrated as it heals. You can use it up to three times a day. Apply a bandage and change it daily If your toenail fully falls off, or partially falls off and a large portion of the nail bed is exposed, keep it covered with a clean bandage and change it daily, says Hullings. Choose a non-adherent bandage, meaning one that covers the exposed nail bed with a pad that doesn’t fuse to the healing tissue, preventing further damage and painful removal. A standard Band-Aid works well, says Wynes — don’t use hydrocolloid bandages, for example, which are sticky all over. Waterproof Band-Aids stay on my toes better and for longer compared to standard ones. As my feet get hot inside shoes and socks, or are exposed to warm weather, standard bandages start moving around and peeling off, thus defeating their purpose. Waterproof bandages like Band-Aid’s don’t. They block out dirt and germs in addition to water, stay on even when they’re wet, are flexible to wrap around any toe and have a quilted pad that cushions the nail bed. If your toenail is loose, don’t pull at or cut it off, says Toussaint. Leave it intact and let it fall off on its own. I use adhesive butterfly wound closure strips like these to hold loose nails in place when I wear socks and shoes — I’m uncomfortable when I feel the nail move around and I don’t want it to get caught on anything. Since my nail bed isn’t exposed, I put one end of the bandage on the nail and one end on my skin to secure it. Once the nail fully or partially falls off, I switch to standard bandages. Wear a protective toe sleeve while running You can still run if you have a mild to moderate case of runner’s toe, but it’s important to take proper precautions so your case doesn’t get worse. Beyond fixing the issue that caused you to get the condition in the first place, Wynes recommends wearing silicone sleeves on the affected toes, including on top of bandages if you’re using them, to protect and cushion nails as they heal. ZenToes designed these soft gel covers to protect toes with partially or fully missing nails from pressure and friction. You get six in a pack, all of which are reusable and washable: two large covers for big toes and four small covers for smaller toes. They’re thin, so they won’t make your socks or sneakers feel tighter, and they’re flexible to move with your feet. You slip the covers on your toes, and they have a snug fit and extend beyond the nail to help them stay on your toes. If they’re too long, you can cut them for a custom fit. How do you prevent runner’s toe? Correcting the issue that gave you runner’s toe is the only way to prevent it in the future. Below are the main factors doctors recommend paying attention to. If you suspect your runner’s toe was caused by something that’s not on this list, see your medical provider. Wear properly fitting sneakers More often than not, sneakers that don’t fit properly are the culprit when it comes to runner’s toe, says Toussaint. Shoes that are even the slightest bit too small, narrow, big or wide can become a problem over time, so visit your local shoe or running store to get your feet professionally measured. Expert fitters can tell you the size, width and toe box size they recommend, and even analyze your gait and arch type to suggest specific sneakers or insoles. A few basic fit tips: get your feet professionally measured at night when your feet are most swollen, and make sure there’s always at least one thumb’s width of space between your longest toe and the top of the shoe, says Wynes. Wear breathable, moisture-wicking socks Sweaty, hot, damp socks can aggressively rub against and damage your toenails, as well as cause your feet to slide around in your shoes, jamming the toenails into the top and front, says Toussaint. To avoid both of these problems, wear socks made from a breathable, quick-drying material that allows for constant airflow, preventing heat and moisture buildup. I only wear Feetures Elite Max Cushion socks when I run. They have just enough padding to keep my feet comfortable, but not so much that they make my sneakers feel tight. And despite being quite cushioned, they don’t make my feet hot or hold onto moisture — they’re made with ventilated fabric that wicks away moisture and allows for constant airflow. The running socks hug my arches and are slightly compressive to give them extra support, and the toe is seamless to prevent blisters. They also never slip down while I’m running, and the tab at the back of the ankle puts a barrier between my skin and shoe to prevent rubbing. Toesocks can also help prevent runner’s toe, although wearing them takes some getting used to. Fabric separates each toe, which prevents skin-on-skin friction that often causes pressure through heat and moisture buildup. Injinji makes popular toesocks for runners. This pair is lightly cushioned and designed with sweat-wicking fabric, as well as a mesh top panel to allow for constant airflow. There’s also a heel tab on the back to prevent the socks from slipping down while you’re moving, and the sneaker from rubbing against your skin. The sock’s internal band hugs your arches to help stabilize them. Tie shoelaces in a runner’s knot Tying your shoelaces in a specific way might not seem revolutionary, but I promise it makes a huge difference. All the doctors I talked to recommended doing the runner’s knot (also called the heel-lock tie or marathon loop), which locks the midfoot and heel in place so the foot can’t slide forward and jam against the top and front of your shoes, says Hullings. Here’s how to do the heel-lock tie, with a video for reference. Lace normally (criss-cross style) until you reach the second-to-last eyelet.Take each lace and put it through the top eyelet on the same side. Don’t pull the laces all the way through — make loops or “bunny ears” on each side.Take the left lace and put it through the loop on the right side, and take the right loop and put it through the loop on the left side.Pull (but not too tightly) and tie. Keep your toenails short with smooth edges The longer your toenails are, the more likely they are to jam against the top and front of your sneakers. Trim them often to keep them short, and use a file to smooth them out, preventing sharp edges from getting caught on your socks. These single-blade cutters cleanly slice toenails without crushing, cracking or splitting them, and they use less force compared to a typical pair, according to the brand. “They give the top of my nails the smoothest look and feel, and cut everything in one even swoop,” says NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown. “There’s also a little compartment attached that catches nail clippings as they come off, so you don’t have to worry about them flying everywhere.” The cutters have a built-in safety stop and anatomically correct blade to stop you from trimming too short, and the short lever is positioned close to the cutting point, giving you more control and top-down visibility. As you shape and smooth out your nails, a glass file like this one better seals the layers of your nails at the edges, preventing splitting over time, according to the brand. They’re also reusable without losing their grit — you just clean them with soap and water as needed. Bona Fide Beauty’s glass file comes with a protective case. Meet our podiatry experts At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also ensure that all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and with no undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Dr. Jacob Wynes is a podiatric surgeon and an associate professor of foot and ankle surgery for the University of Maryland School of Medicine.Dr. Kristin Hullings is an assistant professor of clinical orthopaedic surgery and sports medicine at Temple University’s Lewis Katz School of Medicine.Dr. Rull James Toussaint is the chief of the foot and ankle division in the department of orthopaedic surgery and sports medicine at the University of Florida College of Medicine, where he also serves as a clinical associate professor. I also extensively cover running and sneakers. For this article, I interviewed three doctors about runner’s toe, how to treat it and the best ways to prevent it. I’m also a long-distance runner who has experienced runner’s toe numerous times, so I shared solutions that have worked for me. articles.title: Lib Dems and Reform in war of words over alleged shove
articles.summary: The Lib Dems claim Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accuses the party of "lying".
articles.body:
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.

The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.

Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.

The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".

The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."

Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.

However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph .

The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.

Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.

In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.

"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.

"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."

Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."

Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."

The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.

In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.

"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.

A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

articles.title: Hundreds of GP surgeries lose online services after Silicon Practice collapse
articles.summary: It will cause huge disruption in some parts of England and Wales, say GP leaders.
articles.body:
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.

Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.

Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk , have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.

GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.

Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.

"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."

Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.

Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".

Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them.

"When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams.

"It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."

She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.

articles.title: Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes charges over fatal Colorado firebombing
articles.summary: Mohamed Sabry Soliman, who is already serving a life sentence over the fatal 2025 attack, changed his plea in the federal case on Thursday.
articles.body:
A man who had already been found guilty of firebombing a group of protesters advocating for the release of Israeli hostages in the US state of Colorado has now plead guilty to federal hate crime charges.

Prosecutors said Mohamed Sabry Soliman threw Molotov cocktails at the group of demonstrators in June 2025 - injuring at least 12 people, one of whom died.

He plead guilty in May to 101 state charges, including first-degree murder - resulting in a sentence of life in prison - but initially pleaded not guilty in the federal case.

Prosecutors want Soliman to be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years over the federal charges, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

United States Attorney Peter McNeilly said the sentencing recommendation was driven by what the victims wanted.

In light of the plea, McNeilly said Soliman had dropped motions seeking to keep his family from being deported from the US in case they needed to be witnesses in his case.

Authorities said Soliman planned the attack for a year, watching videos on explosives before driving from his home in Colorado Springs to the Boulder protest.

While he hurled the Molotov cocktails at the crowd on 1 June, 2025, he shouted "Free Palestine". The group were members of Run for Their Lives in Colorado, which met weekly to support the release of Israeli hostages taken by Hamas during the 7 October attacks.

Karen Diamond, 82, died from injuries caused by the attack three weeks later. Her family said her husband, Lou, was also severely burned and had to recover for a month in a hospital burn unit.

Soliman, an Egyptian national, told police after he was arrested that he wanted to "kill all Zionist people", according to court documents.

He came to California in 2022 on a non-immigrant visa that expired in February 2023, according to CBS.

The firebombing escalated concerns about antisemitic violence in the US, taking place shortly after a fatal shooting outside a Jewish centre in Washington DC.

articles.title: Nearly half of U.S teens ages 13 to 17 say they’ve gambled in the last year, survey finds
articles.summary: More than 40% of teens ages 13 to 17 say they’ve gambled in the past year, according to a new survey, raising red flags about the popularity of betting among minors.
articles.body: More than 40% of American teens ages 13 to 17 say they’ve gambled in the past year, according to a survey published Wednesday, raising red flags about the popularity of betting among minors. Researchers from Rutgers University’s Center for Gambling Studies surveyed nearly 1,700 Americans between 13 and 27, and found that 52.5% of the respondents said they had gambled. Among those 17 and under — for whom gambling is illegal — the share was nearly 43%. “We are living in a time where anyone can have a casino or sports book in their pocket,” said Lia Nower, the director of the Rutgers center and lead author of the new report. “Now teens who should be playing sports are betting on them, often with family members.” Nower and her colleagues conducted the survey over the spring and early summer, describing the effort as the first national gambling prevalence study of U.S. adolescents and young adults in nearly 20 years. The report does not offer a comparison to past gambling trends, so it is difficult to assess whether the results represent an increase. In an interview, Nower referenced a 2007 study in the Journal of Gambling Studies, which found that 68% of respondents between 14 and 21 had gambled in the past year. The numbers can’t be compared apples to apples, however, as the methodologies and age ranges differed. Still, the prevalence of problem gambling in the new report appears to be higher than in the 2007 study. Of the respondents who reported gambling activity, nearly 40% “showed symptoms of problem gambling,” the report says, and 10% could be considered “high-risk problem gamblers.” Among teens 17 and under who said they gambled, about 11% were classified as “high risk for problems,” according to the report. “Gambling is no longer confined to casinos and lottery tickets. It is increasingly embedded in video games, sports broadcasts and other products young people can access,” Nower said. “We have worried this would increase rates of problem gambling among youth. Now we know. It does.” She described the findings as cause for alarm. “Gambling has an operant conditioning component that results in some people getting addicted over time,” Nower said. “Most people who start young bet small amounts with friends or family and then increase the number of activities, frequency and amounts wagered over time.” The Rutgers researchers classified gambling fairly broadly to include 21 activities, such as street games, lottery tickets, games of skill, cryptocurrency trading and prediction markets — “anything where money is wagered,” Nower said. That definition was based on a similar one in a 2017 study, she added: “Staking money or something of material value on an event having an uncertain outcome in the hope of winning additional money and/or material goods.” The most common gambling activity among those surveyed was scratch-off tickets, followed by bingo and lottery tickets. Of the respondents who reported gambling, around 20% said they had participated in sports betting. A smaller share said they bet in prediction markets (just over 6% of gamblers). It’s been more than eight years since the Supreme Court issued the landmark ruling that struck down a federal law that prohibited states from allowing gambling on sports. The change touched off an explosion of betting across America. Some form of sports gambling is now legal in 39 states and Washington, D.C. Mobile gambling apps, which include standard casino options and sports, have become particularly popular in recent years. Baseball fans who watched the World Series over the last week were inundated with ads for prediction markets like Polymarket, Novig and Kalshi. The trading platform Webull occupied a spot on the Tampa Bay Rays uniform. Nower said her findings “should be a wake-up call for parents, educators, health professionals and policymakers.” “We cannot wait until young people reach adulthood to begin addressing gambling-related harm,” she said. “By that point, we will have very high rates of problem gambling. Prevention must start earlier, screening must be broader, and public policy must recognize that the gambling environment has changed dramatically.”

articles.title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
articles.summary: BBC Verify examines how much the welfare system costs and the options the government could use to reduce it.
articles.body:
Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.

Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.

Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.

BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.

The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.

The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.

However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.

Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control.

But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.

Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards .

So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.

Many also see a specific problem regarding the growing number of young people in the welfare system claiming benefits, including PIP.

Official figures show the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neets) has risen by around 230,000 since 2019 to just under one million.

Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.

His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025 . It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.

What could cutting the benefits bill mean?

Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.

In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.

However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.

So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.

The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.

There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25 , so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.

There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access , although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.

Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.

This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits , suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.

This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.

However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.
