articles.title: 5.9 Million French Press Coffee Makers Recalled After Reports of Burns
articles.summary: Bodum is recalling nearly 6 million of its popular French press coffee makers after reports of the glass carafe breaking and burning consumers. See the list.
articles.body: One of the most popular brands of French press coffee makers is recalling nearly 6 million units of its products due to risk of “serious burn injury,” according to a notice from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Bodum is voluntarily recalling eight models of its French press coffee makers with replaceable glass carafes after the company identified 70 reports of the carafes breaking and almost 50 reports of people being burned while using them, the CPSC notice says. “As a family-owned business, Bodum takes particular pride in making household products — including coffee and tea makers — that are both high quality and affordable, and we have used that formula to benefit millions of families worldwide for the past 72 years,” the company said in a statement. “To maintain the trust and satisfaction of our customers, we pride ourselves in using high-quality materials and ensuring our products meet or exceed all relevant safety standards,” the statement continues. The recall affects eight models of French press coffee makers with replaceable glass carafes, some of which have been on the market since 1974. Here’s what to know about the Bodum French press recall. Which Coffee Makers Are Being Recalled? The recall specifically affects Bodum French press coffee makers, which have 8-cup and 12-cup replaceable glass carafes. These models are included in the recall: Bistro BrazilCaffettiera Chambord Crema Java Jesper Kenya The recalled coffee makers were in stores and online at Target, Walmart and many other home goods stores. They were sold from 1974 through October 2026 for prices between $15 and $65, according to the notice. Why Are the Bodum Coffee Makers Being Recalled? Bodum is voluntarily recalling its French press coffee makers after the company identified some issues with the glass carafes. There have been 70 reports of the glass carafes breaking, during use, the CPSP notice says, including 48 reports of burns. However, the recall is not related to a defect of the product, but rather with the way people use may use their coffee makers, as the glass can break down over time. Consumers should not be using metal utensils, such as spoons, inside the glass carafe, the CPSC notes, because that can lead to damage and breakage. “This recall is an opportunity to reinforce warnings against using a cracked or damaged carafe and in particular, against using metal spoons to stir coffee in the glass carafe, which can damage the glass and lead to breakage during use,” Bodum said in its statement. “While the rate of reported incidents involving carafe breakage during use is extremely low, especially considering that Bodum has sold millions of these products in the U.S. for decades, this recall will further encourage the safe use of our French Press Coffee Makers.” What to Do if You Have One of the Recalled Coffee Makers If you have one of the recalled Bodum French Press coffee makers, you should stop using metal utensils to stir inside the glass carafe, the CPSC says. Instead, contact the company to receive a free Bodum-designed plastic stirring spoon to use with the French press, the company said in a statement. “Going forward, these products will be sold with the plastic stirring spoon and an additional warning label,” the statement continues. “As the North American market leader in this product category, Bodum is taking these additional actions to reinforce our instructions and warnings about the safe use of the product.” The CPSC also notes that consumers should not use cracked or damaged glass carafes, adding that using metal utensils can lead to damage to the glass.

articles.body:
Dearborn, Michigan – Jake Lang, a far-right provocateur in a bulletproof vest, shouts anti-Muslim obscenities on a bullhorn outside a rally featuring former US President Barack Obama in Detroit.

His associates, wearing crusader-themed accessories – including a tin shield featuring a black cross – hold campaign signs for Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, who is in a close race with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

If it weren’t for the bigoted slogans, the people lining up around them to attend the campaign event for El-Sayed and other Democrats could have mistakenly thought the protesters were in Halloween costumes.

“Get the f*** out, Muslims,” Lang shouted. “The crusade is coming. Self-deport.”

Lang may appear like a fringe agitator. But Muslim American activists say the bigotry he is spreading is going mainstream, especially in the context of the Senate race in Michigan.

Anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed have been perpetuated at the highest level of the US government, including by President Donald Trump and his cabinet members.

Suehaila Amen, a prominent Arab and Muslim advocate in the Detroit area, said bigotry against her community is reaching an all-time high.

“They make immediately post 9/11 look like a walk in the park for us. This has been absolutely disgusting to witness,” Amen told Al Jazeera.

One of Lang’s allies, Pastor Lorenzo Sewell, is an official faith adviser to the Rogers campaign.

Sewell helped Lang organise an anti-Muslim march in the Detroit suburb of Dearborn – home to a large Arab and Muslim community – in August.

Abdullah Hammoud , the mayor of Dearborn, said the city – which has long been a target for anti-Muslim provocateurs – has been receiving an increased number of threats in recent months.

“The general public is unaware of how many threats are aimed towards the city of Dearborn on a daily basis, via social [media], via our dispatch when they’re calling 911 or calling our call centre, and lobbing these threats against the residents of the city each and every single day,” Hammoud told Al Jazeera.

While the Rogers campaign did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment about the Republican candidate’s links to Sewell, Rogers defended his focus on El-Sayed’s background, saying it was for national security.

“This is not about the way you pray; it’s the way you think,” Rogers told reporters after his debate with El-Sayed earlier this month.

Local leaders say their community is not cowering in the face of such threats and Trump’s near-daily attacks, and is pushing back through civic engagement and rallying around the El-Sayed campaign.

“Trump is a fascist,” Hammoud told Al Jazeera. “I think the best thing we can do, the best response, is to send Abdul to the US Senate, somebody who’s got two doctorates, someone who is a son of this country, a son of the state, someone who is the captain of his high school team … I think that that’s the best response that we can give fascism.”

Trump has repeatedly mocked El-Sayed’s name, misrepresenting it as Mohammed, and called the Democratic candidate a “jihadist”.

Amen said Arab and Muslim Americans are used to being targeted for their names, but when the president does it, it legitimises bigotry and racism.

“It’s not just some loser that lives around the block who may call you a racist expletive; it’s the loser who lives in the White House,” she said.

Amen added that Arab and Muslim communities are going about their daily lives and organising politically despite the escalating attacks, stressing that they reject attempts to cast them as foreigners or outsiders.

“We are an integral part of the fabric of this nation, whether people like it or not,” she told Al Jazeera.

As the Senate race intensifies, Rogers has been baselessly accusing El-Sayed of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood , Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Last month, Rogers went as far as agreeing with a social media post calling El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official, a “terrorist”.

Trump has suggested that El-Sayed would be a physical threat to the Capitol, saying that he would want him to go through a metal detector .

At an event in western Michigan earlier this week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr incorrectly claimed that Arabs do not produce literature or science and “don’t win Nobel Prizes”. He argued that the Muslim Brotherhood – which only briefly held power in Egypt between 2012 and 2013 – has destroyed Arab civilisation.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz joined in on such attacks, describing El-Sayed as a “jihadist leprechaun”.

Cruz warned that El-Sayed, a Michigan-born and raised father of two with a medical degree and a doctorate in public health, could end up on the Senate Intelligence Committee and endanger national security.

“If I am correct that he is a passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood, there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result,” he said.

On Wednesday, Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy invoked Dearborn – one of the safest and fastest-growing cities in Michigan – to drum up fear of immigration.

“Look at what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan, for God’s sake. We’re not going to let that come to our state of Ohio,” he said.

El-Sayed, who is of Egyptian descent, has avoided focusing on the attacks, calling them “deflections and deceptions”.

It’s not clear how attacks linked to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and Arab heritage will affect the race.

About 38 percent of respondents in a survey of potential voters conducted by Michigan State University said a candidate being a Muslim would make them less likely to offer support to their campaign.

After a Trump rally for Rogers in Port Huron, northeast of Detroit, where the president spent most of his nearly two-hour speech attacking El-Sayed, some attendees appeared to agree that El-Sayed may be a threat to national security.

As the US president spoke, shouts of “traitor”, referring to El-Sayed, erupted from the crowd.

Trump supporter David Beamer, whose son died in the 9/11 attacks in 2001, spoke at the event and questioned El-Sayed’s American identity.

“Abdul has a birth certificate. The birth certificate says he’s a citizen of America. You know what? A birth certificate doesn’t make you an American,” Beamer said.

Al Jazeera asked Duane Crempa, a 72-year-old Republican in a Batman mask who attended the Trump speech on Sunday, whether he believes that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” as Trump claims.

Crempa said he is a good judge of character. “Yeah, there is something not right with him. That’s all I’ll say; there’s definitely something not right,” he added.

Jermaine Miller, who also was at the rally, told Al Jazeera he hopes El-Sayed is not a “terrorist”.

“But I mean, it sounds convincing, but it is believable,” he said of Trump’s allegations that the Democratic candidate is a “jihadist”.

In the Detroit area, Arab and Muslim advocates say the issue is bigger than a Senate seat, arguing that such rhetoric endangers their communities and risks ripping the social fabric of the state.

“We’ve seen the increase in hate marches and hate speech and people being very comfortable sharing their hateful views online and coming into our city and harassing people for no reason – people who are just trying to live and function in this country,” Amen said.

“It’s been tremendously heartbreaking to watch our community constantly have to question why people are maliciously maligning them in public.”

Earlier this year, two gunmen killed three people outside a mosque complex in San Diego in southern California in what authorities said was a hate crime.

Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, who represents Dearborn and parts of Detroit, said she fears for her two Muslim boys, Adam and Yousif, amid the rise of hate with the election campaign.

“Yesterday, we were all watching the football game, and we literally had to turn off the ads every time in between [plays] because we didn’t want our babies to see these awful, racist ads,” Tlaib told Al Jazeera.

“It’s awful to live this way right now.”

With petrol in Michigan nearing record highs, Arab and Muslim advocates say their communities are being scapegoated to cover up the shortcomings of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran.

Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, communication director for American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), said the attacks against El-Sayed amount to “disgusting Islamophobia” that serves as a distraction.

“Abdul El-Sayed’s name is a visibly Muslim name, and it’s being treated as inherently suspicious, as if a Muslim American cannot willfully execute their duties as an active member of Congress to protect the American people,” Abdelrahman told Al Jazeera.

At the Trump rally in Port Huron, one of Trump’s allies appeared to weigh El-Sayed’s candidacy against petrol prices.

Brian Pannebecker, a retiree from an auto manufacturing company Trump invited to the stage on Sunday, stressed that Michiganders need to vote for the Republican ticket.

“I don’t care if they’re paying a buck and a half more a gallon for gasoline. That is no excuse to vote for a socialist Islamist for the US Senate,” Pannebecker said.

articles.body: A month later, Republican leader Bo French posted a racist comment targeting Indians and expressed how unapologetic he was; details emerged about how the students reacted and how they wanted the university authorities to issue a stern reply immediately, but then all they got was a measured statement that did not even have Bo French's name. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” French, the Republican running for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, wrote in a post featuring a photo of the students. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”The students were Indian-origin US citizens.35 hours after the post created a storm on social media, UT-Austin President Jim Davis issued a statement saying that all UT students were Longhorns. He did not touch upon the race issue.The Texas Tribune reported that within hours, Davis' office received 22 emails urging him to speak up. “Silence in the face of bigotry is complicity,” wrote Rohan Reddy Gupta, a 2020 graduate. “A clear, public condemnation of these racist remarks is not optional; it is a moral obligation.”3 professors stepped up, wrote email to studentsThree Indian-origin Computer Science professors stepped up and wrote an email to the students. “We want to express our support for all students regardless of ethnicity, and tell you that if you need someone to talk to, we are here to help,” computer science professors Keshav Pingali, Vijay Chidambaram and Chandrajit Bajaj wrote in an email to students. Texas Tribune reported that Pingali said growing hostility toward Indian Americans prompted the message. He also recognized former students in the photo French included in his remarks and was distressed to learn some feared attending future football games. Students later visited Pingali’s office to thank him, saying they appreciated knowing faculty members were paying attention, he said.UT's student body drafted a message but then...Texas Monthly reported that Dean Young, a member of the UT Student Government, drafted a message condemning Bo French.“Recent public comments attributed to Bo French have generated discussion and concern among members of the University community regarding the treatment and representation of South Asian students,” Young wrote in one draft. “Student Government stands with all students, regardless of race, as proud Longhorns.”The resolution was sponsored by a bipartisan group of eleven other student government representatives, including one affiliated with the campus chapter of the conservative Turning Point USA. But a few days after filing the resolution for consideration by the broader student government body, Young was contacted by Jennifer Zamora, the new faculty adviser to student government. Young told Texas Monthly that Zamora advised that they should not mention French in the resolution because he is a candidate for political office. Zamora cited a prohibition on political speech by university-sponsored organizations and said French’s comments had by then sparked a much larger debate that should be the focus of the resolution. “It’s not just Bo French who is saying these things,” Young recalled being told. “All over social media, there is hate about South Asians.”You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2021, Detroit renovators Keith Bynum and Evan Thomas bought an abandoned house for $1,000, gave it a Palm Springs-inspired makeover and sold it for $81,000; the reported profit was about $35,000
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of Keith Bynum and Evan Thomas as they turn neglected Detroit homes into beautiful starter homes for first-time buyers, showcasing their success with a stunning Palm Springs-inspired renovation.
articles.body: Compared to most American cities, Detroit has more vacant homes. Due to years of population decline, unpaid property taxes, and foreclosures, the city and its land bank now own thousands of empty homes, many of which are on blocks where neighbours still reside and take pride in their neighbourhood. That presents an opportunity for buyers willing to take on extensive repairs. The renovation approach later became the basis of a business and the HGTV series Bargain Block, after Keith Bynum and Evan Thomas moved from Colorado to Detroit in 2017.HGTV's Bargain Block premiered on April 14, 2021, following Keith Bynum and Evan Thomas as they renovated vacant Detroit houses into furnished starter homes. The Palm House featured in the second episode, titled Dormer and Palm, which aired on April 21, 2021. The pair bought the Palm House for $1,000, set a renovation budget of about $45,000 and sold it for $81,000. MEAWW reported an estimated profit of $35,000 on this property, although that figure was not an independently audited accounting of all costs.The Palm House's designMEAWW reported that the Palm House was in better shape than many of the pair's other projects, allowing them to set a renovation budget of about $45,000. Bynum gave the home a bright, palm-themed design intended to evoke a vacation getaway. The look combined tropical accents, colourful details and secondhand furnishings rather than reproducing Palm Springs' desert architecture literally. Bynum often gives each property a distinct theme and incorporates thrifted objects and his own artwork into the design. A clear theme also helps at the point of sale. It's a smart way to stand out in a price category when a lot of properties look the same, and buyers comparing a $79,000 listing with other restored homes nearby will recall the one that felt like a home.How $1,000 homes are createdThe Detroit Land Bank Authority's Own It Now program offers eligible vacant properties with a minimum offer of $1,000. The homes are sold as-is, and buyers are required to renovate them and ensure they are occupied, according to the City of Detroit's description of the program. The Palm House's reported purchase price was also $1,000, but the program rules alone do not establish that this particular property was sold through Own It Now. A low purchase price does not mean a home is ready to live in; the buyer must account for the repairs required.The pair were drawn to the contrast between Detroit and its suburbs. Evan Thomas told Seen magazine that houses selling for roughly $200,000 in Ferndale could be available for far less in Detroit. By May 2022, Pride Source reported that Bynum and Thomas had renovated nearly 30 homes. Their budgets varied by property. In a feature published by HGTV, Bynum said they typically spent about $45,000 on a house.How the profit built upMEAWW reported that the Palm House was listed for $79,000 and sold for $81,000, or $2,000 above asking. The outlet estimated its profit at about $35,000 after accounting for the $1,000 purchase price and the $45,000 renovation budget. It separately reported that the Dormer House sold for $99,000, with an estimated profit of $25,000. These are outlet-reported estimates rather than independently verified financial accounts. Actual profit could differ after closing costs, property taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance and the owners' labour are considered. Any TV flip comes with a word of caution. A genuine profit also has to factor into closing costs, property taxes, insurance, utilities and the hours the owners put in working, so these numbers are a rough guide rather than a definitive accounting.The pair's approach was to buy vacant houses at low prices, renovate them within set budgets and resell them at prices intended to remain accessible to first time buyers. In a 2022 announcement, Warner Bros. Discovery said the first season of Bargain Block attracted more than 20 million viewers, suggesting strong audience interest in the show.The Palm House illustrates how a low purchase price can be followed by substantial renovation costs. The reported profit estimate depends on the purchase price and renovation budget, but it does not provide a complete account of every expense. The Detroit Land Bank's sales programs also require buyers to rehabilitate properties bought through them, so a low initial price is only the beginning of the investment.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Arab voice doesn’t count’: Jewish Israeli blocs reject Palestinian support
articles.summary: Palestinian voters could decide Israel’s future, but its political class refuses to accept their mandate
articles.body:
Few certainties have emerged from Israel’s parliamentary elections. The diverse coalition of Israel’s self-styled ‘Zionist’ opposition remains short of a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud appears to be the largest party, but its electoral bloc has not secured enough seats to form a government.

What is not in doubt, however, is the surge in turnout from Palestinian citizens of Israel, which has established Arab parties as a pivotal bloc in the parliament, potentially one able to determine which of the rival camps forms a government, if either is willing to work with them.

Anger over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and what analysts have described as the overt racism of its governing coalition helped drive Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in large numbers.

An estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters in Israel turned out for Tuesday’s election, marking a surge in participation by a community that accounts for about 21 percent of the population.

The turnout has given the two main electoral lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List – a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining who forms the next government.

However, rather than acknowledge that groundswell of support, Israel’s leading politicians have sought to either delegitimise their vote – attributing it to foreign interference – or somehow cast Palestinians exercising their democratic right as an “attempt to steal the election”.

Framing the result as a bid to secure the “Islamisation of Israel”, Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party has gone so far as to call on Israel’s internal security service, the Shin Bet, to investigate the possibility of foreign election interference into the large-scale Palestinian turnout. In doing so, they appear to have thrown the legitimacy of the Arab vote into question and tainted any future attempt by the opposition to ally with the Arab parties.

Despite denouncing Netanyahu’s government as corrupt, incompetent and damaging to Israel’s international standing, much of Israel’s Jewish-led opposition has remained reluctant to embrace the support of Palestinian parties to remove him from power.

The left-wing Democrats have been the likeliest to cooperate with the Palestinian parties, while other opposition figures have either resisted such an alliance or stopped short of rejecting allegations that foreign actors helped engineer the surge in Palestinian voter turnout.

On election night, former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid ruled out sitting alongside Palestinian parties in government, despite having relied on their support during their brief 2021–22 government.

On Thursday, another leading member of the opposition, Avigdor Lieberman, the hard-right leader of Yisrael Beytenu, also ruled out forming a coalition with Palestinian parties. He said he would sit alongside “neither Bibi nor Tibi”, using Netanyahu’s established nickname and invoking Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al party – part of the Joint List – as a stand-in for the wider Palestinian bloc.

“It was clear from campaigning that there was going to be a large turnout,” said Orly Noy, who stood for the Palestinian-dominated Balad party. “The [governing] coalition had shown there were no red lines in Gaza and Palestinians in Israel sensed they might be next. People also just couldn’t face another term of soaring crime and a police force headed by [far-right National Security Minister] Itamar Ben-Gvir.”

“What few rights Palestinians had have been slipping away since October 7. The last tool they had in their toolbox – the only thing they had that was equal to everyone else – was their vote, so they used that in massive numbers, but even that now seems to be being undermined and delegitimised,” she said.

With all ballots counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, while the anti-Netanyahu Jewish opposition bloc has 48. However, with the 19 seats held by Palestinian parties, the majority in parliament is against Netanyahu.

“Why are the opposition and the press even thinking of this as a three-way split? In any other rational democracy, people would be framing this as an overwhelming victory for the opposition and a rejection of Netanyahu, but we’re not doing that,” Noy said.

“Instead, we’re hearing elements of the opposition talking about joining with Netanyahu in some kind of National Unity government. That’s both a measure of how racist these parties are, when they won’t align with Arabs to form a majority, as well as how profoundly undemocratic they are,” she said.

Political differences do exist between an opposition that deliberately frames itself as Zionist and a Palestinian minority whose claim to equal national and civic rights is seen by some as a rejection of that. But underlying that disagreement is a fundamentally different vision of Israel’s future, according to political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg.

“Given that much of Israel’s mainstream politics rests on the assumption of Jewish supremacy, I think it’s understandable that the Arab vote is seen as a challenge,” he said of a sentiment that many argue has been state policy since the 2018 Nation State Law , which enshrined the right to national self-determination as exclusive to Jewish people.

“There are very different ideas at play of what it means to be a citizen of Israel and of how Israel should be governed and for whose benefit,” he said. “These are fundamental differences, of course they are, but they can’t disguise the racism underpinning all.”

“They want to form a government with only Jewish voices,” said Mauricio Lapchik, Hebrew campaign director for the Joint List. “If the numbers of these results were in a different country, in a democratic country, I think it would be crazy to think that they will not be able to say that they won the elections, having this majority. But only in Israel, because the voice of the Arabs do not count as the voice of the Jews, we cannot talk about a victory.”

articles.title: Florida dad who swam to tangled seagull and was carried away from shore drowns
articles.summary: Stone Romberg drowned after swimming out to untangle a seagull from his fishing line when an ocean current swept him away from the Florida shore.
articles.body: A father who swam out into the sea to help untangle a seagull from his fishing line drowned and died after an ocean current swept him away, Fox 5 Atlanta reported. Atlanta area native Stone Romberg was fishing at his home in the Florida Panhandle when he noticed the seagull caught in his fishing line, Fox 5 reported. The 31-year-old father of two swam out to try and untangle the bird, but his hook and the bird got stuck to his hand while he tried to help. As he tried to swim to shore, an ocean current carried him further out to sea where he tragically drowned. "Our hearts are broken for everyone who knew and loved him," a GoFundMe set up for his family reads. MOM OF 2 WHO DIED RESCUING SONS DURING BAHAMAS SNORKELING TRIP IS IDENTIFIED Romberg was the manager of chair services at a local condominium complex and "was known by a lot of our owners and guests," according to the GoFundMe. A Facebook page for his workplace also shared that he will be remembered "for his kind heart, hard work, and willingness to always lend a hand." THREE MEN GET 158 YEARS EACH FOR MURDERING AMERICAN AND AUSTRALIAN SURFERS, DUMPING BODIES IN MEXICAN WELL "His kindness left a lasting impression on everyone who knew him, and he will be deeply missed," the post also read. The GoFundMe set up for his family, who relied on him for financial support, has raised $138,714 as of Thursday afternoon. He is survived by his wife Taylor and his one-year-old and three-year-old girls. articles.title: India ready to share its battle-tested expertise with Asean partners to boost joint capabilities: Rajnath
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India’s extensive expertise in counter-terrorism is not theoretical classroom knowledge but it is an experience hard-earned on the ground
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India’s extensive expertise in counter-terrorism is not theoretical classroom knowledge but it is an experience hard-earned on the ground through decades of directly confronting complex, cross-border security challenges, defence minister Rajnath Singh said in the Philippines on Thursday.Addressing the 13th ASEAN Defence Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM) - Plus in Cebu, Rajnath underlined that “every strategy of India has been tested, refined and proven in the crucible of real-world operations” and that India stands fully prepared to share its practical, battle-tested experience with ADMM-Plus partners through joint exercises, capacity-building programmes, and robust intelligence sharing to strengthen collective capabilities. He reaffirmed the country’s commitment to collective regional security and eradication of terrorism in all its forms.Rajnath said this proactive, battle-tested doctrine was decisively demonstrated during Operation Sindoor, when India dismantled terrorist infrastructure and enforced a non-negotiable red line against state-sponsored terror. He stressed that counter-terrorism remains an important area of cooperation under the ADMM-Plus framework, and India and Malaysia are co-chairing the experts’ working group on counter-terrorism for the 2024 to 2027 cycle.Rajnath highlighted that by deploying frontline warships, India has successfully escorted thousands of merchant vessels and thwarted dozens of high-seas hijackings, extending protection to commercial shipping irrespective of flag or nationality. He termed the security of commercial shipping as India’s responsibility. “In an era where global trade routes face complex transnational threats, India stands ready to move beyond rhetoric. There is a need for effective action, regular operational presence and international cooperation. India will continue serving as a reliable net security provider in the Indian Ocean Region and the wider Indo-Pacific,” he said.The minister highlighted the importance of youth engagement in strengthening India-ASEAN defence cooperation, stating that the shared demographic profile and aspirations of the young populations provide a strong foundation for deeper regional partnership. He proposed the establishment of a dedicated defence ‘Youth Bridge’ to enhance institutional people-to-people connectivity, promote digital innovation and facilitate capacity building in line with ADMM-Plus initiatives.On the sidelines of ADMM-Plus, Rajnath met Japanese minister of defence Shinjiro Koizumi, and Australian minister for defence Richard Marles and posted a picture with them. “JAI: Japan, Australia, India”, the defence Minister posted on X, with him holding hands of both Marles and Koizumi, as he stood in the middle.At the forum, the minister reiterated that India attaches importance to ASEAN centrality and a secure, open, inclusive, resilient and rule-based Indo-Pacific, where peace and stability are not just aspirations but a result of collective commitment. He stated that its strategic engagement with ASEAN is long-term and rooted in shared interests, mutual respect and practical cooperation. He recalled that the second ASEAN-India defence ministers’ informal meeting in Kuala Lumpur in Oct last year reaffirmed the commitment to advancing the defence and security components of the ASEAN-India Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and the ASEAN-India Plan of Action for 2026 to 2030.On the theme of 13th ADMM-Plus ‘Navigating Our Future, Together’, Rajnath stated it resonates with India’s foreign and defence policy paradigms as well as its civilisational ethos of ‘Sarve Bhavantu Sukhinah’ (May all beings be happy) that reflects the aspiration for the happiness, prosperity, and well-being of all the people across the world. “This theme reminds us that our greatest strength lies in our solidarity and the shared ability to leverage our geographic, economic and strategic diversity. India believes in an international system built on mutual trust, co-operation, and collective responsibility. It is this precise collaborative spirit that empowers us to overcome the challenges to peace and order,” he said.The minister described maritime cooperation as crucial to India’s engagement with ASEAN during 2026, highlighting New Delhi’s designation of 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation and the conduct of the second ASEAN-India Maritime Exercise. He emphasised that India does not merely preach the tenets of international maritime law; it is a steadfast practitioner of global laws concerning maritime security. “Our commitment to ensuring the freedom of navigation and safeguarding global Sea Lines of Communication is backed by a continuous, decades-long operational legacy. Since 2008, the Indian Navy has maintained an uninterrupted, active presence in highly volatile corridors like the Gulf of Aden, without coercion or unilateral actions that undermine the rights of other nations,” he said.Rajnath said India’s emphasis on the rule of law, particularly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and its advocacy for freedom of navigation and overflight are not directed against any country but are meant to safeguard the collective interests of all regional stakeholders who depend on open sea lanes and stable maritime governance.

articles.title: After buying a Pennsylvania farm in 1850, James McCray sold an oil lease to fund a nearby well; the venture brought him $70,000, and he later refused $1 million
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of James McCray, a farmer who sold an oil lease to fund a nearby well, turning a $70,000 profit while navigating the volatile oil market and rejecting a staggering $1 million offer for his land.
articles.body: Before the oil boom, farmers in Pennsylvania's Oil Creek valley relied on crops and livestock, and the surrounding hillsides could be difficult to farm. Edwin Drake's well near Titusville in August 1859 helped establish commercial oil drilling in the region. The discovery changed the value of nearby land as operators began searching for productive ground. James S. McCray, who had bought a farm in 1850, became one of the landowners whose fortunes were transformed by the oil boom.Farmers who leased their land were among the first to benefit from the oil boom, according to the American Oil and Gas Historical Society. Its history of early wells along Oil Creek describes how the valley and surrounding hillsides were rapidly leased or purchased as operators sought promising drilling sites. McCray's farm stood on a bluff just east of Petroleum Centre, close to the developing oilfield.From pay at the mill to farmJohn J. McLaurin's historical account describes McCray as the son of a farmer, born in 1824 near Titusville. At 22, McCray set out on his own with two dollars in his pocket and spent three years working at a sawmill on the Allegheny River. By 1850, he had saved enough to buy a team and begin farming. His property later became part of the oil boom that followed Drake's 1859 discovery. McCray's first oil venture involved selling an interest in a lease to raise money for further drilling.Selling a lease to drill a wellMcLaurin's account says McCray's first oil venture was a share in a two-acre lease at Rouseville. He sold that interest to finance a well on the nearby Blood farm, alongside his own property. McLaurin reported that this venture brought McCray $70,000. His account, Sketches in Crude Oil, is a historical work about the early petroleum industry rather than a novel.A lease was merely the right to drill for a fee. In the 1860s leases changed hands nearly as if they were shares. Selling one to pay for another was an early method of raising capital, and it was risky: a dry hole would have left him with nothing. It also meant McCray learned how the money flowed before he had to make a decision on what to do with his property.McLaurin reported that McCray turned down an offer of $500,000 for his 80 acres in 1865. Friends reportedly regretted the decision for years. A well drilled on the top of the hill was too shallow to reach the oil-bearing layer and was thought to be dry, delaying further development there for about five years. The 1865 offer came after commercial oil drilling had already begun in the region.Saying no to $1 millionInterest in Petroleum Centre revived in 1870 when Jonathan Watson drilled a productive well on the nearby Dalzell farm, close to the southern boundary of McCray's property. The strike renewed demand for leases on McCray's own farm. McLaurin reported that prospective lessees were offering a bonus of $1,000 per acre plus half the oil produced, but McCray could not meet even a tenth of the demand. These terms described leases, not offers to purchase the land. In 1871, he reportedly refused an offer of $1 million for his farm. The Venango Museum's history of the 1870 oil boom describes how Watson's well renewed interest around Petroleum Centre.McCray's decision to hold oil rather than sell it immediately carried a different set of risks. In 1871, when prices were around $3 a barrel, he reportedly refused to sell below $5. McLaurin recorded that McCray bought, hired and built iron tanks to store about 200,000 barrels while waiting for higher prices. Leakage, evaporation and taxes reduced the value of the stock. He declined offers of $4, $4.50 and $5 a barrel before eventually selling most of the oil for about $1 to $2 a barrel.McCray faced different risks when holding land and storing oil. The value of his property depended on the productivity of the wells and the demand for leases, while stored crude could lose value through leakage, evaporation, taxes and falling prices. His decision to hold the oil in anticipation of a higher price left him exposed when the market moved in the opposite direction.By the time McLaurin published his account in the 1890s, Petroleum Centre's oil boom had become part of the region's past. McCray's experience illustrates how drilling could transform the value of a farm, while holding crude for a better price exposed landowners to storage costs and a volatile market. articles.title: Congress calls for probe into land deals linked to Shikhar Agarwal; demands CM response
articles.summary: Rajasthan Congress chief Govind Singh Dotasra seeks probe into land deals linked to IAS Shikhar Agarwal, questions halted RIICO auction, demands CM reply.
articles.body: Jaipur: Rajasthan Congress president Govind Singh Dotasra Thursday alleged irregularities in decisions linked to IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal, who was removed from all posts a day earlier, and demanded that Chief Minister Bhajan Lal Sharma make a public statement explaining the govt’s action against him.Dotasra said the IAS officer’s long stint as the chief minister’s secretary warranted clarification on decisions taken during that period also. He flagged land transactions in which properties bought for about Rs 6.15 crore were later leased out at an annual rent of Rs 1.85 crore, calling for scrutiny of the deals. He further sought probes into the alleged halting of a RIICO auction in Daulatpura, and questioned file movements related to Mahindra SEZ and a project involving the Adani Group, asking the state govt to disclose how and why the decisions were made.“Are the Enforcement Directorate, Income Tax Department and Central Bureau of Investigation meant only to target and intimidate Congress? Or, these are to prevent corruption? The govt must demonstrate impartiality in the Agrawal case,” Dotasra said, speaking to the media.Dotasra also claimed bureacuratic infighting has intensified in the state, citing former chief secretary Sudhansh Pant’s mid-term transfer out of Rajasthan and now Agrawal being placed on awaiting-posting orders. Until Wednesday, Agarwal was heading industries, investment, MSME, state enterprises and couple of other departments, as the additional chief secretary. articles.title: Raj maps district-wise industries to link school students with jobs
articles.summary: Rajasthan RCSE maps district industries to link Classes 9–12 vocational students with OJT, visits and placements, boosting local job options, especially for rural girls.
articles.body: Jaipur: Rajasthan Council of School Education (RCSE) is mapping industries across districts to connect students in Classes 9 to 12 enrolled in vocational courses with on-the-job training (OJT), industrial visits and placement opportunities.The initiative aims to expand career options, particularly for girls from rural areas who often opt for traditional trades such as sewing and salon services due to limited exposure and mobility.RCSE commissioner and state project director Rashmi Sharma said the department was preparing a roadmap for school-industry partnerships. “We are mapping industries near schools because parents often hesitate to send girls far from home due to safety concerns. We want students to access training and job opportunities close to where they live,” an official said.The Alwar-Bhiwadi belt, for instance, offers opportunities to partner with automobile companies for guest lectures and placements, the official added. OJT would familiarise students with workplace requirements and help reduce job attrition.The benefits of vocational training are already evident. Aarti Verma, whose father works as a labourer, studied retail at Govt Shardul Senior Secondary School in Kishangarh, Ajmer, and now works as a hotel front office assistant.Chanchal Prajapat, employed at a retail store, said training had improved her confidence in interacting with customers, arranging products and understanding their needs.Rajasthan offers vocational education in 17 trades across more than 4,000 schools, covering around five lakh students, including 2.84 lakh girls and 2.05 lakh boys.Potential industry partners span healthcare, textiles, tourism, IT, electronics, banking and retail. articles.title: Fire at Chinchwad housing society forces residents to the terrace to escape smoke; damages 14 vehicles, 1 sustains minor burns
articles.summary: Basement parking fire at Chinchwad housing society in Pune damaged 14 vehicles; 15 residents rescued from terrace, one injured; short circuit suspected.
articles.body: Pune: A fire broke out in the basement parking lot of a housing society in Chinchwad in the early hours of Thursday.It damaged 14 vehicles and forced residents to rush to the terrace to escape the thick smoke. Fifteen stranded residents were rescued by the fire brigade, while one person sustained minor burns. Venkatesh Hardas, head of Pimpri Chinchwad fire brigade, told TOI, “Four fire tenders reached the spot and doused the fire. Prima facie, a short circuit appears to have caused the fire. Our investigation is underway.”Fire officer Gautam Ingawale of Pimpri Chinchwad fire brigade told TOI that the fire broke out around 2 am in the basement parking lot of a four-storey commercial-cum-residential building near Chapekar Chowk in Chinchwad. Two floors of the building housed shops, tuition classes and other establishments, while the remaining two floors were residential. “The building has a single entrance. The fire broke out in the parking lot, and thick smoke entered the flats above, making it difficult for residents to breathe. As they could not get out of the building, they rushed to the terrace.”Firefighters wearing breathing apparatus sets checked all the flats to ensure that no one, particularly senior citizens, was trapped inside. They then reached the terrace, shifted the residents to the terrace of a neighbouring building and rescued them safely. “The fire damaged at least 14 vehicles, including 12 two-wheelers, two cars and a bicycle. A transformer on the building’s premises was also damaged. It took us about an hour to extinguish the blaze completely,” Ingawale said.Senior police inspector Dattatrya Chaskar of Chinchwad police said a resident who sustained minor burns was taken to a hospital. “We are investigating what started the fire.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Pune | Silver Rate in Pune | Bank Holidays in Pune | Public Holidays in Pune | Petrol Price in Pune | Diesel Price in Pune | CNG Price in Pune | LPG Price in PuneStay updated with the latest Pune news. articles.title: After leasing drilling rights on his 71-acre Tennessee farm for 12.5%, Vernon Lawhorn saw an oil strike reportedly bring in $30,000 a month and bought a $6,500 Dodge
articles.summary: Discover how Vernon Lawhorn transformed his 71-acre Tennessee farm into an oil-producing asset, generating $30,000 per month after leasing drilling rights at a 12.5% royalty rate. Learn about the significance of this rare oil strike in a state not traditionally known for oil production.
articles.body: Tennessee has never been a major oil producer, but its smaller wells have supported a modest petroleum industry. That made the experience of farmer Vernon Lawhorn noteworthy. In an October 1980 report, The Washington Post described Lawhorn as a farmer with 71 acres near Oneida who leased drilling rights to Bill Goodwin's partners in return for a 12.5% share of the well. The report said Lawhorn was earning about $30,000 a month from the oil strike and had bought a white Dodge Diplomat for $6,500.The Tennessee Encyclopedia notes that Tennessee has never been a major oil and gas producer, although petroleum has contributed to the state's economy. Oil was found in some shallow wells associated with brine production before the development of the modern petroleum industry. Tennessee's first commercial oil well was drilled in Overton County in 1866, seven years after Edwin Drake's famous Pennsylvania well in 1859.What a 12.5% royalty meantUnder a royalty arrangement, the operator typically pays for drilling and equipment while the landowner receives an agreed share of the value of production. A 12.5% royalty represents one eighth of that value under the lease terms. The 1980 newspaper account reported that Lawhorn leased his drilling rights for a 12.5% share and was earning about $30,000 a month from the resulting oil strike. It did not describe the $30,000 as the well's total revenue, so multiplying that amount by 12.5% to calculate Lawhorn's income would be incorrect. The reported figure should be treated as a contemporary estimate of his monthly earnings rather than an independently verified financial statement.Oil in a little countryTo put this in perspective, a 1940 OneMine document assessing Tennessee’s oil and gas reported the state’s total crude production for that year at just over 15,000 barrels, a drop of roughly 36,000 barrels from 1939. A large part of the decline was caused by the shallow pools of Clay County, where in 1940 just 3,000 barrels were marketed compared with more than 37,000 in 1939. That’s the whole state’s annual production, and one productive well somewhere else might duplicate that in days.Tennessee has also had some substantial producing wells. Hornet Corporation reported that its Wayne Brown No. 3 well in Overton County was drilled to a depth of 1,557 feet in 1994 and produced more than 274,000 barrels of oil before it was plugged. The company described it as the largest producing oil well in the state's history. These figures come from Hornet's own account of the well.What the strike changedThe 1980 account of Lawhorn illustrates how a landowner could benefit from leasing drilling rights to an independent operator. The reported monthly income was substantial, but the available account does not provide a full financial breakdown or establish how long the payments continued. The story remains an example of the opportunities and uncertainty that accompanied Tennessee's oil development.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
